17:A task, a prompt in Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform, is sent straight away while its lane is free. While its lane is busy, it waits in its queue instead, in the order it was sent, keeping its mode and attachments, until its turn comes.
18:When a task is actually sent, the spec is built ahead of it, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, the task showing "Building" until the build is over; then its hidden anchor is compiled and run. It heads the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) as the latest task, and is saved in the prompt history, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. A prompt that fails to compile or run fails its task, and doesn't stop its queue.
19:A task whose mode runs in a container, a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up, is run in one, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says, showing "Preparing environment" while its image is built; one that can't be, as where Podman isn't installed, fails as a task that can't be run does, and is never run on the host instead. A Code task and a Chain prompt's code step always run on the host, and never need Podman. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over, however it ended, the spec is built again on the host, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says.
21:#### Lanes
23:Tasks run in two lanes, the code lane and the spec lane, each with a queue of its own, so work on the spec never waits on work on the code, or the other way round. A task sent in Code goes to the code lane, and one sent in Spec to the spec lane. A Chain task's steps each go to the lane of the work they do, as the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor) says: its spec steps to the spec lane and its code step to the code lane, even though they were sent together from the Chain tab. A task sent in Freeform may change either, so it goes to the code lane, and is only sent while no task runs in either lane; while it runs, both lanes are busy, and prompts for either queue behind it.
24:A lane is busy while a task of its own is building, compiling, or running, or a Freeform task is. So a Spec task sent while only a Code task runs is sent straight away and runs beside it, and a Code task sent while only a Spec task runs does the same; a task only queues behind a task of its own lane. At most one task runs in each lane, and each lane's queue sends its prompts one at a time, first to last. Both lanes belong to the same project, and a project's lanes only ever send into that project.
28:A question, a prompt in Ask, never queues: it runs straight away, even while the harness is working on a task or other questions, joins the questions stacked above the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s tabs, and is saved among the questions asked. Every question runs in a container that holds the code, the spec source, and the compiled reference, each read only, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says, and fails, never running on the host, where that can't be done.
32:While a task is running, more can be sent to it, as to a terminal session, from the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s "Send to task", as it says. It goes to the latest task, whose output is shown; a task running in the other lane, among the previous tasks, isn't sent to. What is sent is written as a hidden anchor and compiled like any prompt, unless the task was sent from Freeform, when it goes just as it was typed, with its attachments, its references, attachments, and Slice toggle included, so it can reference the spec, but the spec isn't built first, and its systemPrompt isn't sent, since the run already has the one it began with. It goes to the running task's run as a message of its own, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, and is not a task of its own: it doesn't head the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list), isn't among the previous tasks, and can't be resent. It is shown in the task's output and kept with its record, as the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor) says. A message that fails to compile isn't sent, and a notification titled "Could not send to the task" says why, what was typed going back into the input. A message whose task ends before it can be sent is queued instead, as a task, so nothing typed is lost.

The prompt resent stays where it is. A prompt whose mode isn't known, saved before modes were, is resent from the chat input's selected tab. 52:A cancelled task keeps the output it had so far, and its status reads "Cancelled", as the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) shows, in the history as much as in its header. It adds no commit note, and any change the harness had already made to files is left as it is. Its lane's queue carries on after it, as it does after a task that fails, sending the next prompt waiting in it, and the next task carries on the same conversation. The task in the other lane, and questions, are not cancelled with it.

.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md:60:A prompt sent in Chain runs as steps, each saved in the history as a task of its own: first the Chain task itself, which writes the spec; then the same prompt sent to Code, told what the spec step did; and, when the chain asks for a post-build spec update, the same prompt sent to Spec once more, told what the code step did. Each step knows the one it was sent from, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Only the steps the chain sends itself belong to it; a task sent to the other mode by hand, or resent, from one of its steps is a task of its own.
.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md:61:Each step runs in the lane of the work it does, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says: the Chain task and its spec follow-up in the spec lane, the code step in the code lane. A step is sent once the step before it finishes, never before, and goes to the head of its lane's queue, ahead of the prompts already waiting there, so it runs as soon as that lane is free, and straight away if it already is. The lane it leaves is free for its own queue meanwhile, so a Spec task sent while a chain's code step runs runs beside it. A step waiting for its lane shows in the queue like any prompt, and can be cancelled there, ending the chain. A step whose chain step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent.
.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md:62:Each step also runs where the work of its lane runs, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says: the spec steps in a container holding the spec and no code, the code step always on the host, with its protected locations. Each carries on its own lane's conversation, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, so a step is told what the step before it did only through its prompt: the Chain prompt as typed and that step's final output, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](./mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says.
.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md:69:The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working. It is always the most recent task still active: of the tasks under way, building, compiling, or running, in either lane, the one sent most recently. Only while no task is under way is it the task that finished most recently, or, before any has finished, the one sent most recently. A finished task never heads the view while another is under way: when it finishes while a task in the other lane still runs, that task heads the view in its place at once, and the task that finished goes among the previous tasks. So with two Chain tasks sent one after the other, once both their spec steps have finished, the first chain's code step heads the view while it runs, not the second chain's finished spec step, and the second chain's code step heads it in turn once it is sent. A task still running in the other lane that is not the latest is among the previous tasks, shown running there, as any previous task is. Whichever task heads the view, its header and output show as they do for a task just sent, and the previous tasks, their row's count, and the chain grouping follow it. The header shows its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead. At its right, a Resend button sends it again, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. The header shows the prompt the task was sent with, however much is sent to it while it runs; what is sent is shown in its output.

use /lib
use /ui
from ./chat-input import ChatInputScope
from ./message-list import MessageList
from ./queue-list import QueueListScope
from /scope/container-environment import ContainerEnvironmentScope
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/no-project import NoProjectStateScope
from /scope/open-projects import OpenProjectsScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/ask-conversation import AskConversationScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /ui/components/history-list import HistoryListScope
from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope

export ui-component PromptEditor:
    concept: {PromptEditorConcept}

concept PromptEditorConcept:
    pitch:
        An interface for sending tasks to a local coding harness like Claude
        Code, written directly with compiled-on-depand Piton.

    shape: {PromptEditorShape}

shape PromptEditorShape:
    description:
        Not a chat. Each prompt sent is a task for the harness, tasks can
        queue, and each task shows its output until it finishes. There are no
        message bubbles.

    basicDesignAndLayout:
        The @{MessageList} fills the body's Chat tab: all the space between
        the body's tab bar and the @{ChatInputScope} along the bottom. From top to bottom it holds the
        previous tasks row, the header, holding the latest task and every
        other task under way, one of them selected and shown in full and the
        rest as compact rows, as the @{MessageList} says, the selected task's
        output, and the queue.

        Before any task has been sent, the space shows a hint instead, which
        wraps when the view is narrow. It reads
        "Write a prompt below. Enter adds a line; Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it."
        or, while no project is open, as the @{NoProjectStateScope} says,
        "Open a project to start prompting."

    chatHistory: @{MessageList}

    previousTasks:
        Previous tasks are a @{HistoryListScope} along the top of the view,
        listing every task sent. Its row counts every task but those the
        header shows, the latest, which heads the view, and any other under
        way: "No previous tasks", "1 previous task", or
        "N previous tasks", and each offers Resend. Expanded, the list takes the place of the latest
        task and its output, and the row reads "Back to the latest task".

        Every task in the list has a checkbox at the left of its heading,
        before its status, and clicking it selects or deselects the task
        without opening or closing it. Shift-clicking one selects every task
        between it and the one last clicked, never deselecting any; with none
        clicked before, it selects or deselects that one as a plain click
        does. The selection is kept while the list is closed and opened again,
        until it is cleared or sent. Each open project keeps its own, as the
        @{OpenProjectsScope} says.

        While any task is selected, the row shows the batch actions at its
        right, in place of nothing: "N selected", muted, counting every task
        selected, then "Send N to Spec" and "Send N to Code", small ghost
        buttons with a swap icon, each tinted the colour of the mode it sends
        to, then "Clear", which deselects them all. Send N to Spec counts, and
        sends, the selected tasks that offer Send to Spec, and Send N to Code
        those that offer Send to Code, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says; each
        is shown only while its count isn't zero. Tasks that don't offer it,
        sent in Chain or Freeform, whose mode isn't known, already sent to the
        other mode or being sent there, marked done, or complete, can be
        selected, and are counted in "N selected", but neither action sends
        them. Clicking an action never opens or closes the list.

        A batch action sends each of its tasks to the other mode, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says for one, oldest first: the first starts
        straight away while its lane is free and the rest queue behind it in
        that lane, so they run in the order they were first sent, each saved in the
        history as a new task. Once sent, the tasks it sent are deselected,
        the rest of the selection is kept, and the list stays as it was, still
        expanded, with nothing opened. With no project open, it sends nothing,
        a notification says a project must be opened first, and the selection
        is kept.

    previousTaskFilters:
        While the previous tasks are expanded, a filter bar sits along the top
        of the list, beneath their row and above the first item, on the tab
        bar's background with the theme's line beneath it, and scrolls with
        nothing: it stays put as the list scrolls. It holds two groups of
        small toggle chips, the second set 12 pixels apart from the first,
        wrapping onto another line when the bar is too narrow. Each chip
        reads its label and, muted after it, how many previous tasks match
        it on its own, whatever other chips are on; the latest task, heading
        the view, is never counted.

        The first group filters by the mode each task was sent in, one chip
        per task mode in the @{PromptModesScope}'s order, "Code", "Chain",
        "Spec", and "Freeform", each tinted its mode's colour while on, its
        border in that colour and its background a faint tint of it. The
        second group's chips take the theme's accent the same way while on.
        The second filters by where a task stands with the other mode, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says, with "Can send to Spec" for tasks that
        offer Send to Spec, "Can send to Code" for those that offer Send to
        Code, "Sent" for those already sent to the other mode or being sent
        there, and "Marked done" for those marked done by hand.

        With no chip on, which is how the list starts, every previous task
        shows. Within a group, the chips on combine as either, so a task
        shows when it matches any of them, and the two groups combine as
        both, so with chips on in each, a task shows only when it matches one
        in each. Clicking a chip turns it on or off, and a "Clear" button at
        the bar's right end, shown only while any chip is on, turns them all
        off. A chip that would show no tasks is still shown, its count 0, and
        can still be turned on.

        Filtering only hides tasks from the list; it changes nothing about
        them. A chain whose steps are hidden in part keeps its parent row
        above the steps still shown, and is hidden with its parent only when
        none of its steps shows. Session dividers show only above a session
        with a task shown. The row's count still counts every previous task,
        and while any chip is on, what the row reads, the count, or "Back to
        the latest task" while the list is expanded, is followed by " · N
        shown", N counting the previous tasks the filters show. A hidden task
        stays selected if it was, and is still counted in "N selected" and
        sent by the batch actions; an open task that is filtered out closes.
        With every task filtered out, the list reads "No previous tasks match
        these filters", muted, centred. The filters are kept while the list is
        closed and opened again, and each open project keeps its own, as the
        @{OpenProjectsScope} says, but they are not saved with the project.

    chainedTasks:
        A prompt sent in Chain runs as steps, each saved in the history as a
        task of its own: first the Chain task itself, which writes the spec;
        then the same prompt sent to Code, told what the spec step did; and,
        when the chain asks for a post-build spec update, the same prompt sent
        to Spec once more, told what the code step did. Each step knows the
        one it was sent from, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says. Only the
        steps the chain sends itself belong to it; a task sent to the other
        mode by hand, or resent, from one of its steps is a task of its own.

        Each step runs in the lane of the work it does, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says: the Chain task and its spec follow-up in
        the spec lane, the code step in the code lane. A step is sent once the
        step before it finishes, never before, and goes to the head of its
        lane's queue, ahead of the prompts already waiting there, so it runs
        as soon as that lane is free, and straight away if it already is. The
        lane it leaves is free for its own queue meanwhile, so a Spec task
        sent while a chain's code step runs runs beside it. A step waiting for
        its lane shows in the queue like any prompt, and can be cancelled
        there, ending the chain. A step whose chain step before it failed or
        was cancelled is never sent.

        Each step also runs where the work of its lane runs, as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says: the spec steps in a container
        holding the spec and no code, the code step always on the host, with
        its protected locations. Each carries on its own
        lane's conversation, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, so a step
        is told what the step before it did only through its prompt: the
        Chain prompt as typed and that step's final output, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says.

        In the previous tasks list, a chain's steps are grouped under one
        parent item, so they read as parts of a single chain. The parent is a
        heading row in the list, tinted the Chain colour, as the
        @{PromptModesScope} colours it, a little more strongly than a single
        task's tint: a joined chain icon, the first line of the prompt, and at
        its right how many steps it has, "2 steps" or "3 steps". Its status is
        the chain's as a whole: Running while any step runs, Failed or
        Cancelled if a step was, and otherwise that of its last step. It has
        no checkbox, Resend, or Send to the other mode of its own, and
        clicking it doesn't open anything.

        Beneath it, each step stays an item of its own, exactly as any
        previous task is, with its checkbox, status, Resend, and whatever
        else a task offers, opening onto its own prompt, table, and changed
        files. The steps are indented from the parent, joined to it by a
        thin line in the Chain colour down their left, from the parent's
        heading to the last step, and each is labelled by what it did,
        "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", in that step's mode colour,
        before its prompt, which leaves out the prompt's first line when it
        is the parent's. They are listed in the order they ran.

        A chain is listed where its first step was sent, oldest first like
        every other item; tasks sent while it ran, such as questions or tasks
        of the other lane run between its steps, are never listed within it,
        and are listed after the chain, in the order they were sent. A chain's
        steps are found by which step each was sent from, not by being next to
        each other in the history. A chain still running, or one whose later
        steps haven't been sent yet, shows as many steps as have been, and
        a step still running shows as it would anywhere. When the latest
        task, heading the view, is a step of a chain, that chain's earlier
        steps are still grouped under its parent in the list, the parent
        saying the rest is the latest task. A session divider never falls
        between a chain's steps: it goes above the chain's parent. A step
        from the history whose chain can't be worked out, as when the step
        it was sent from is missing, is listed as a task of its own.

    header:
        The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working.
        It is always the most recent task still active: of the tasks under
        way, building, compiling, or running, in either lane, the one sent
        most recently. Only while no task is under way is it the task that
        finished most recently, or, before any has finished, the one sent
        most recently. A finished task never heads the view while another is
        under way: when it finishes while a task in the other lane still
        runs, that task heads the view in its place at once, and the task
        that finished goes among the previous tasks. So with two Chain tasks
        sent one after the other, once both their spec steps have finished,
        the first chain's code step heads the view while it runs, not the
        second chain's finished spec step, and the second chain's code step
        heads it in turn once it is sent. A task still running in the other
        lane that is not the latest is among the previous tasks, shown
        running there, as any previous task is. Whichever task heads the
        view, its header and output show as they do for a task just sent,
        and the previous tasks, their row's count, and the chain grouping
        follow it. The header shows
        its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the
        hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the
        harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it
        has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead. At its right, a
        Resend button sends it again, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says. The
        header shows the prompt the task was sent with, however much is sent to
        it while it runs; what is sent is shown in its output.

        However long the compiled prompt, a prompt sent with its spec slices
        included, the header lays out only what is in view: the prompt is
        split into its blocks of markdown, paragraphs, headings, lists, and
        code blocks, each drawn as it scrolls into view, as the rows of a
        table are, so a long prompt costs no more to show, scroll, or
        animate than a short one. The header is as tall as the prompt up to
        where it starts to scroll.

    rawPrompt:
        Beside the latest task's Resend button, a small ghost button with a
        code icon, whose tooltip says "View the raw prompt", opens a modal
        showing exactly what the harness was given for the task, once it has
        been sent: nothing rendered, nothing hidden. Clicking it never opens or
        closes anything else in the header. Until the task has compiled, it
        is disabled, its tooltip reading "No prompt sent yet". Only the
        latest task's header has it; previous tasks and questions don't.

        The modal is titled "Raw prompt", with the task's mode, its hidden
        anchor's name, and the harness it was sent to beneath the title, or
        "Harness not recorded" for a task saved before the harness was. The
        anchor's name is shown for a Freeform task too, though its header
        hides it. It shows two sections, each headed and each with a Copy
        button that copies that section's whole text, disabled while the
        section has none to copy:

        \\
        - System prompt: the system prompt as the harness received it, with
          every placeholder filled in and every injected prompt in its place,
          the spec-reading prompt, and the code-to-spec prompt with the code
          task's prompt and final output, as the
          @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says; or "No system prompt" when none was
          sent, as for Freeform.
        - User prompt: the compiled prompt the harness received, with its spec
          slices when it was sent with them.
        \\

        For a harness that takes no system prompt of its own, where it is given
        ahead of the prompt, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, the modal
        shows the one text it was given, headed "Prompt", with a single Copy
        button. A prompt sent with attached images ends with a third section,
        "Attached images", listing the path of each saved image, one to a
        line, with its own Copy button. Messages sent to the task while it ran
        are not part of it; they are shown in its output.

        The text is shown as plain monospace text, wrapped, selectable, and
        scrolling within the modal, laying out only what is in view however
        long it is: it is drawn in rows of 16 lines, each laid out as it
        scrolls into view, so a selection is made within one row and can't be
        dragged across rows, while Copy always takes the whole section. The
        modal is 85% of the window's height, and 90% of its width up to 1000
        pixels. Pressing Escape,
        clicking outside it, or its close button closes it.

        What it shows is what was sent, not what the templates say now: the
        system prompt as sent, and the harness it was sent to, are saved in the
        task's history record beside its compiled user prompt, for questions as
        much as tasks, and for a harness given one combined text, the system
        prompt alone, the combined text built again from it exactly as it was
        sent, so the modal shows the same for a task restored
        from the history. A task saved before this was recorded shows its
        system prompt as "Not recorded".

    queue: @{QueueListScope}

    projects:
        Tasks, the queue, and the auto-send switch belong to their project, as
        the @{OpenProjectsScope} says: the view shows the tasks and queue of the
        project on screen, while those of other open projects carry on in the
        background. A project's queues only ever send into that project.

    buildingTheSpec:
        A task builds the spec before it is sent, as the @{PromptModesScope}
        says, since the task may be the one to fix the spec, its output
        starting with an error saying the build failed when it does. A Spec
        task, or a Chain prompt's spec step, builds it again on the host once
        it is over, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says, so the next step, and
        every task after it, reads the spec as that run left it.

    history:
        Every task sent is saved in the prompt history with the project's data,
        as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, and its record once its run is over.
        Opening the project, the first time in a launch, brings back every
        task in order, with its output
        replayed from that record. The record keeps each message sent to the
        task while it ran, as typed and as compiled, in its place among the
        lines the harness printed, so the task comes back as the exchange it
        was, each message a Sent row followed by what came of it. A task with no record shows as
        "Not recorded".

        Every question asked from the Ask tab is logged the same way, but among
        the questions instead, so it never comes back as a task: it comes back
        in the @{AskConversationScope}. The record is saved when the run is
        over, and also when the question is stopped while it runs, with as
        much as the harness had done. A question
        that fails before it reaches the harness is logged too, with the error
        in its record.

    chatInput: @{ChatInputScope}

content.text:
Yes, there was a reason: the spec told the code to do it. It said a chain's next step "goes to the head of its lane's queue, ahead of the prompts already waiting there". So whenever a chain's spec step finished, its code step jumped ahead of every Code prompt already waiting. That included other chains' code steps queued earlier, which is the out-of-order sending you saw. I changed the rule; `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

## What changed in the spec

**Chained tasks** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md#chained-tasks`)
- A chain step now takes its place in its lane's queue by when its chain was sent, not when the step itself was ready.
  - It waits behind every prompt sent before its chain, including earlier chains' steps.
  - It goes ahead of every prompt sent after its chain.
- A chain's code step never jumps ahead of a Code prompt or another chain's code step sent before it.
- A Code prompt sent while a chain's spec step is running waits for that chain's code step, so nothing lands between a chain's steps.
- Two chains' code steps run in the order the chains were sent, whichever spec step finished first.
- If nothing sent earlier is waiting, the step runs as soon as its lane is free, as before.

**Saved queue** (`.claude/reference/scope/project-data/index.md#contents`)
- A queued chain step is saved marked with when its chain was sent, so it keeps its place in the queue after a restart.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791224395-ChainModePromptOrderInvestigation.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `PromptEditor`: `#chained-tasks`, for where a step is inserted into its lane's queue.
- `PromptSendingScope`: `#lanes`, for each queue running first to last.
- `ProjectDataScope`: `#contents`, for how `queue/` files are named and marked so their order survives a restart.
